title: Newman Elementary Students March for Red Ribbon Week in Laredo
excerpt: Students at B. P. Newman Elementary in Laredo marched for Red Ribbon Week, joining a national drug-prevention campaign that runs through October 31.
content:
Students at B. P. Newman Elementary School in Laredo took to the streets in red this week, marching for Red Ribbon Week — the national drug-prevention campaign that asks young people to pledge to live drug-free. KGNS reported the march on October 26, as schools across the country marked the annual observance.

At Newman, the week carries a sharper local focus: the campus is observing Red Ribbon Fentanyl Poisoning Awareness Week from October 26 through October 30, and October is Fentanyl Poisoning Awareness Month at the school. The message on campus is blunt — one pill can kill — and it lands in a community that has seen fentanyl deaths prosecuted in federal court here in Laredo in recent weeks.

Red Ribbon Week is observed nationally from October 23 through October 31, and this year's theme is “Make A Difference. Be A Hero. Stay Drug Free.” The campaign, run by the National Family Partnership, traces back to the 1980s and honors a fallen Drug Enforcement Administration agent. It has grown into one of the largest drug-prevention campaigns in the country, with schools marking it through marches, assemblies, themed dress days and classroom lessons.

Why a march matters

A march is a visible pledge. When elementary students walk together in red, the statement is aimed as much at the adults watching — parents, neighbors, drivers passing by — as at the children themselves. Prevention researchers consistently say the same thing: the earlier and more often children hear a clear, consistent drug-free message from their school, their family and their community, the better it sticks.

That is especially true for fentanyl. Unlike the drug threats of past Red Ribbon Weeks, fentanyl poisoning does not require a habit — a single counterfeit pill can be fatal, and pills that look like prescription medication can carry a lethal dose. School campaigns that name fentanyl specifically, as Newman is doing, are responding to that reality rather than to a generic warning.

Questions worth asking

A week of red ribbons is a start, not a strategy. Parents and residents should ask: what drug-prevention curriculum runs at Newman and other United ISD campuses the other 51 weeks of the year? Are parents getting the same fentanyl information students are — including how to recognize counterfeit pills and where to find naloxone? And are local schools connected to the treatment and recovery resources in Webb County when a family needs help, not just a slogan?

Those are questions for the district, for campus administrators and for the community organizations that support them. The students, for their part, have already done the visible work: they showed up, they marched, and they said no out loud.
